name: Agbekor
story: An Anlo Ewe war dance from Ghana, now performed at funerals and festivals. The gankogui bell timeline holds everything together while sogo and atsimevu interlock.

name: Gahu
story: Borrowed by the Ewe from Yoruba-speaking peoples via Benin. Lighter and more celebratory than Agbekor, and often the first ensemble rhythm a drum-class learns.

name: Kpanlogo
story: Invented in 1960s Accra by Ga youth — a conga-based social dance that fused traditional Ga drumming with highlife and rock, now Ghana's de facto national rhythm.

name: Kuku
story: Originally played for women returning from fishing trips. Now the first djembe ensemble rhythm taught worldwide — driving, joyful, endlessly danceable.

name: Soli
story: The initiation rhythm of Malinke Guinea — it accompanies the dance-stories of young people crossing from childhood to adulthood. Sacred in its traditional context.

name: Dununba
story: The dance of the strong men — acrobatic, muscular, led by the booming dundunba drum the rhythm is named after.

name: Fanga
story: A welcome rhythm spread across the African diaspora in the 1960s by Babatunde Olatunji. The doors open, the drums speak, the guests enter.

name: Adowa
story: The most widespread Akan dance — performed at funerals, royal gatherings, and festivals. Graceful hand-and-foot gestures tell proverbs through movement.

name: Bembé 6/8
story: The "standard pattern" — the 12/8 bell timeline that traveled from Yorubaland to Havana to Salvador and anchors half the African diaspora's music.

name: Djembe Standard
story: The archetypal djembe accompaniment — tones and slaps interlocking over the kenkeni pulse. Mande culture's most traveled rhythmic export.

name: Tiriba
story: A joyful rhythm traditionally played for women's celebrations — harvest, fertility, coming-of-age. The sangban's bell pattern is what you'll hear first and remember longest.

name: Yankadi
story: Young men and women face each other in two lines and take turns stepping forward to express interest. Gentle, patient, and an ideal first djembe ensemble rhythm.

name: Makru
story: Yankadi's fast partner. The lead drummer signals the transition and the whole dance explodes — one of West African music's most thrilling gear-changes.

name: Djansa
story: A rolling, forward-moving Mande celebration rhythm played at weddings and naming ceremonies. The dundun interplay is what makes it unmistakable.

name: Sunu
story: A swaying, storytelling rhythm. The sangban's rocking bell creates a cradle for the drums and singers to lean into.

name: Bobobo
story: The northern Ewe's most accessible recreational dance — simpler than Agbekor or Gahu, and usually the first rhythm drum-class newcomers learn.

name: Atsiagbekor
story: The complete ritual form of the Ewe war dance — slow processional before a fast dance of combat. Some scholars treat Agbekor and Atsiagbekor as the same tradition seen from two angles.

name: Gadzo
story: A gentle Ewe rhythm tied to everyday work and gathering. Ideal for learning how the standard 12/8 bell locks the supporting drums into place.

name: Tokoe
story: A festive Ewe rhythm where the kidi weaves syncopations between every accent of the bell. The energy is pure celebration.

name: Bata — Shango
story: The fire-and-thunder rhythm for Shango, orisha of lightning. The three-drum Bata trio speaks Yoruba — here we collapse it: okonkolo timeline on HH, iya lead on KK, itotele response on SN.

name: Dundun / Talking Drum
story: The hourglass tension drum squeezed under the armpit bends pitch to mimic Yoruba tonal speech — here a framework groove for the iya dundun to "speak" over.

name: Apala
story: Yoruba Muslim social music, popularised by Haruna Ishola in the 1940s–60s. No melodic instruments — only drums, thumb-piano, and voice.

name: Highlife (Ghana)
story: The sikyi bell timeline runs the whole of Ghanaian highlife — the cosmopolitan, horn-driven sound of E.T. Mensah and the guitar-band era.

name: Afrobeat (Tony Allen)
story: "I play the drums as if I am four people." Tony Allen built Afrobeat's floating pocket by displacing the snare off the backbeat and weaving the kick around it.

name: Sabar
story: The Wolof griot's drum family. The lead nder shouts rhythmic "bakks" — spoken-sentence phrases — that the dancers must answer with specific steps.

name: Mendiani
story: The virtuoso female solo dance of the Malinke — a young girl chosen as "mendiani" performs athletic, elegant variations on the lead drummer's calls. Danced only by pre-pubescent girls; retired once they come of age.

name: Bolon
story: Bolon is both the instrument — a three-string bass harp once carried by Mande warriors to war — and the slow, stately drum cycle that accompanies its songs of heroism.

name: Wassoulou
story: Southern Mali's hunter-harp tradition, reinvented by women — Oumou Sangaré and peers built a global pop style on the kamale ngoni. Earthy, cyclical, deeply feminist.

name: Lamba
story: The foundational griot rhythm — the cycle under which Mandinka jalis praise kings and ancestors on the kora. Every jali learns lamba before any other piece.

name: Kiti Dende
story: A gathering rhythm — played to call the village before a ceremony begins. The dundunba stomps the forward figure; the djembes fill the spaces with rolls.

name: Ogun (Yoruba)
story: The rhythm for Ogun — orisha of iron, warriors, and the clearing of paths. The bell strikes like hammer on anvil; the iya leads attack calls.

name: Oya (Yoruba)
story: Oya rules the wind, storm, and the gates between worlds. Her rhythm is restless, whirling — every beat seems to twist away before it lands.

name: Oshun (Yoruba)
story: Oshun is the river, beauty, fresh water, love. Her rhythm flows — a sweet, sensual bata pattern that ripples rather than strikes. The slowest and most seductive orisha rhythm.

name: Gadzo (Slow)
story: The slow processional half of the Ewe Gadzo tradition — drawn-out bell hits, the war-dance held in meditative suspension before the acceleration begins.

name: Akom (Fang)
story: From Gabon's Fang Bwiti initiates — a cyclical 6/8 accompanying night-long ancestral contact rites. The mongongo mouth-bow carries the melody; drums and rattles drive the trance.

name: Kpelle Pepper Dance
story: Hot-footed — the Kpelle name it for pepper because dancers mime stepping on hot coals. A tight, interlocking groove documented by Ruth Stone in 1970s Liberia.

name: Lamb (Senegalese Wrestling)
story: Laamb is Senegalese wrestling — a national sport of stadium-sized crowds and mystical preparation. The sabar ensemble hammers out attack calls as wrestlers dance into the ring.

name: Gumbe
story: A Creole dance that traveled out of 19th-century Freetown and took root from Senegambia to Jamaica. The square-framed gumbe drum anchors a rolling 4/4 with a habanera bass pulse.

name: Tabanka
story: A Guinea-Bissau carnival rhythm — satirical processions where neighborhoods compete with costumed critiques of the year's politics. Stomping 2/4 over conch-shell calls.

name: Halam (Fulani / Wolof)
story: The Halam / xalam — a four- or five-string skin-bodied lute carried by Fulbe and Wolof griots across the Sahel. Blues scholars trace the American banjo back to this instrument's 6/8 praise cycles.

name: Bembé 6/8 (Yoruba rotation)
story: One of two common rotations of the 7-stroke bell. Where the Mande/Ewe form (see bembe-68) places its strokes at 0,2,4,5,7,9,10, the Yoruba rotation starts on a different pulse of the same underlying pattern and is heard across West African orisha ceremony and, after the Middle Passage, in Cuban Santería.
